input_signals.name: AccrualsPricedOnlyWhenLevered
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), INDICATOR(RATIO(lt, at), 0.65))
input_signals.hypothesis: The accrual-return relation exists only in the levered segment of the cross-section: when liabilities exceed roughly two-thirds of assets, accrual-inflated earnings signal covenant-driven earnings management and imminent reversal, whereas in low-leverage firms accruals mostly reflect benign operating growth and carry no return information.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the double-demeaned product with a one-sided indicator gate removes the flaw the critic identified — low-accrual/low-leverage firms no longer share a tail with high-accrual/high-leverage firms, since unlevered firms are pinned at zero in the middle of the sort. The long-short spread is therefore an accrual sort executed exclusively inside distressed firms, which is the cleanest available univariate test of conditional pricing, and coverage stays full because the indicator is defined for every firm with lt and at.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), oancf ), at ), 1 ), indicator( ratio( lt, at ), 0.65 ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsInFirmWorstRevenueYear
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), dp), at), 1), TS_RANK(NEG(GROWTH(sale, 1)), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Operating distress is best identified relative to a firm's own revenue trajectory: when sales growth is the worst in five years, working-capital accruals cannot reflect benign expansion and instead indicate unsold inventory, stretched credit terms, and imminent write-downs.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing cross-sectional NEG(GROWTH(sale,1)) with its within-firm percentile removes the Lakonishok-Shleifer-Vishny sales-growth premium the critic identified, since a within-firm rank is roughly uniform for every firm and therefore carries almost no unconditional cross-sectional return exposure. This keeps the operating-decline distress dimension — the one economic channel absent from the archive, which so far tests only solvency and liquidity — while making the attribution to the interaction defensible.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( sub( sub( delta( act, 1 ), delta( che, 1 ) ), sub( delta( lct, 1 ), delta( dlc, 1 ) ) ), dp ), at ), 1 ), ts_rank( neg( growth( sale, 1 ) ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWithSalesGrowthBelowIndustry
input_signals.hypothesis: Losing revenue while your industry grows is firm-specific demand deterioration — share loss, product obsolescence, customers defecting — and receivables and inventory accrued against that shrinking franchise will be collected or sold only at a discount.
input_signals.reasoning: Revenue decline was the conditioner behind the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope, but it was measured in raw or within-firm form and so conflated industry downturns with firm-specific failure; industry-demeaning isolates the idiosyncratic component, which is the same transformation that lifted the leverage conditioner from −4.1% to −4.7% with the best Sharpe in the archive. It also avoids the Lakonishok-Shleifer-Vishny sales-growth premium being a sector bet, since the conditioner is demeaned within industry.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), oancf ), at ), 1 ), rank( neg( ind_adj( growth( sale, 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CushionScaledAccrualsWithDemandLoss
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), MAX(ceq, che)), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The damage from an accrual reversal is its size relative to the equity that must absorb it, and its likelihood is highest when the firm is losing revenue to peers, so the two should be measured multiplicatively: accrual per dollar of loss-absorbing capital, amplified by idiosyncratic demand loss.
input_signals.reasoning: This crosses the archive's two structurally different innovations — continuous, unbounded fragility scaling through the equity-cushion deflator (fmb −1.51, Sharpe −0.456) and the best-performing peer-relative conditioner — rather than adding a twelfth rank multiplier to the same asset-deflated accrual. If the combination beats both parents, it establishes that magnitude scaling and conditional amplification capture different aspects of fragility, which is the key open question for the final generation.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), oancf ), max( ceq, che ) ), 1 ), rank( neg( ind_adj( growth( sale, 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: BalanceSheetAccrualsWithDemandLoss
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), dp), at), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Balance-sheet working-capital accruals are informative specifically when demand is deteriorating — that is when a rise in receivables and inventory cannot be explained by growth — which would explain why this accrual leg predicts correctly with revenue-based conditioners and perversely with financing-based ones.
input_signals.reasoning: The balance-sheet leg produced the archive's strongest slope with the within-firm revenue trough (fmb −3.63) but sign-flipped with chronic contraction (α +3.3%) and cash-flow coverage (α +0.7%), and this pins down whether the demand channel is what rescues it, using the conditioner form that has proven most reliable. It also carries the highest coverage in the archive (~0.10 versus 0.08), so a confirmation would give the final generation a broader-sample alternative to the cash-flow accrual leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( sub( sub( delta( act, 1 ), delta( che, 1 ) ), sub( delta( lct, 1 ), delta( dlc, 1 ) ) ), dp ), at ), 1 ), rank( neg( ind_adj( growth( sale, 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsUnderWorstDimensionOfFragility
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), MAX(RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1))))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Financial fragility is determined by the binding constraint, not by an average: a firm that is severely over-levered relative to peers is fragile even if its revenue is growing, and a firm losing revenue share is fragile even at modest leverage, so the relevant amplifier of accrual risk is the *worst* of the two peer-relative dimensions.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a functional-form hypothesis about how distress dimensions aggregate, and MAX is a structure the archive has never used — it directly contrasts with the SUMRANK average of the same two dimensions, so the pair identifies whether fragility is additive or determined by a single binding constraint. Because MAX keeps a firm in the extreme portfolios when either dimension is extreme, the short leg should be populated by genuinely stressed firms rather than by moderate cases that score middling on both, which is the plausible reason averaging has capped this family's alpha near −4.7%.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), oancf ), at ), 1 ), max( rank( ind_adj( ratio( lt, at ) ) ), rank( neg( ind_adj( growth( sale, 1 ) ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DualEstimateAccrualsWithDemandLoss
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(ADD(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), dp), at)), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The cash-flow and balance-sheet accrual measures are two noisy estimates of the same economic quantity; their sum retains the common accrual signal while the estimation errors — articulation differences, mergers, reclassifications — partially cancel, so the extreme portfolios contain firms where both statements agree that accruals are extreme.
input_signals.reasoning: This directly repairs the sharpest anomaly in the archive: the balance-sheet leg with this conditioner gave fmb −3.90 but α −0.6%, exactly what happens when measurement noise widens cross-sectional dispersion without adding return information, while the cash-flow leg gave α −4.1% with fmb −2.03. Averaging the two estimates is an econometric fix with an economic justification, and it should inherit the slope strength of one leg and the portfolio strength of the other.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( add( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), oancf ), at ), ratio( sub( sub( sub( delta( act, 1 ), delta( che, 1 ) ), sub( delta( lct, 1 ), delta( dlc, 1 ) ) ), dp ), at ) ), 1 ), rank( neg( ind_adj( growth( sale, 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CushionScaledAccrualsWithVolatileRevenue
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), MAX(ceq, che)), 1), RANK(VOL(RATIO(sale, at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Fragility has a capacity dimension and an uncertainty dimension: a thin equity cushion determines how much of an accrual reversal the firm can absorb, while an unstable revenue base determines how likely the reversal is, so accruals scaled by loss-absorbing capital should be most damaging where revenue is least predictable.
input_signals.reasoning: Both ingredients worked independently through different channels — the cushion deflator (fmb −1.51, α −3.8%, Sharpe −0.456) and revenue-base volatility (fmb −1.65, α −3.7%) — and neither shares a variable with the other, so their combination tests whether absorption capacity and cash-flow uncertainty are complementary rather than duplicative descriptions of fragility. Unlike the peer-gap conditioners this pairing contains no growth or leverage term, so it provides an independent confirmation route for the family's central claim.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), oancf ), max( ceq, che ) ), 1 ), rank( vol( ratio( sale, at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: EarningsCompositionAccrualsUnderExcessLeverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), ADD(ABS(ib), dp)), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters for a fragile firm is not how large accruals are relative to its asset base but what fraction of its reported earnings is non-cash: when most of the earnings of an over-levered firm is accrual rather than cash, there is nothing available to service obligations and the reported profit will not survive.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the fragile MAX(ceq, che) deflator with a strictly positive, scale-free earnings-composition denominator (|ib| + dp), so it measures earnings *quality* rather than accrual size — economically distinct from every asset-deflated leg in the archive and free of the near-zero-equity outlier risk the critic identified. Combined with the peer-relative leverage gap, the best-performing single conditioner (α −4.7%, t −3.48), it asks whether cash-poor earnings composition is the channel through which leverage amplifies accruals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), oancf ), add( abs( ib ), dp ) ), 1 ), rank( ind_adj( ratio( lt, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ChronicPeerExcessLeverageAccruals
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at)), 0), 3))
input_signals.hypothesis: One year of above-peer leverage can be a deliberate, reversible financing choice, but three consecutive years means the firm has been unable to deleverage and its debt capacity is exhausted, so accrual reversals must be absorbed by write-downs rather than by borrowing.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than twisting the aggregation operator on two known legs, this introduces persistence on the archive's strongest conditioning dimension — a state variable distinct from its level (tested), its one-year change (tested) and its volatility (tested) — and the 0–3 count is well spread rather than compressed toward an endpoint. The economic claim is falsifiable and sharp: if only chronic excess leverage matters, this should beat the one-year peer gap; if the effect is about fresh deterioration, it should be weaker.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), oancf ), at ), 1 ), ts_sum( indicator( ind_adj( ratio( lt, at ) ), 0 ), 3 ) )
